8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":2,"verseId":16,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Motion","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v2_16","number":16,"title":"A Moving Thing Cannot Be Stationary","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If without motion It is not appropriate to posit a mover, How could it be appropriate to say That a moving thing is stationary?"},"philosophy":{"insight":"Since \"mover\" requires motion (v.3-7), a \"moving thing\" is defined by motion. Asserting it is stationary is a direct contradiction — you're saying the moving thing isn't moving. Motion and stationarity are mutually exclusive within the essentialist framework.","madhyamaka":"Garfield: this verse parallels v.3-4 for stationarity. If a mover is defined by motion, stationarity cannot be predicated of it without contradiction. Kalupahana: the verse shows motion and stationarity are complementary dependent designations — asserting one inherently excludes the other. Siderits/Katsura: the argument is swift because the ground was laid in v.3-4.","quantum":"Complementarity (Bohr, 1928): Wave and particle descriptions are mutually exclusive — a quantum system cannot simultaneously exhibit both fully. Measuring wave-like interference destroys particle-like which-path information and vice versa. Similarly, \"moving\" and \"stationary\" are complementary descriptions that cannot coexist.","bridge":"Both frameworks reveal mutually exclusive descriptions. You cannot simultaneously observe wave interference AND particle trajectories. You cannot simultaneously assert motion AND stationarity of the same entity. The descriptions are complementary — each excludes the other.","accessible":"You can't be both asleep and awake at the same time. \"Asleep\" and \"awake\" are defined by excluding each other. Similarly, \"moving\" and \"stationary\" exclude each other. A moving thing can't be stationary — that's a contradiction.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, we identify things as 'moving' or 'stationary.' Ultimately, these designations depend on reference frames and conceptual frameworks — not inherent properties.","commonMisconception":"This is NOT relativism or 'anything goes.' It's showing that motion-designations are framework-dependent — real within their framework, but not inherently fixed."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Complementarity (Bohr)","score":88,"strength":"High","explanation":"Wave and particle descriptions are mutually exclusive — cannot coexist simultaneously. Asserting both simultaneously is asserting: \"this thing that is moving is not moving.\" That's a direct logical contradiction (P and not-P).","realLifeExample":"Saying \"this lit candle is unlit\" is a contradiction. \"Lit\" and \"unlit\" are defined by excluding each other. You can't predicate both of the same candle at the same time."},{"q":"What does this show about stationarity?","a":"Stationarity cannot be found as an inherent property of a moving thing. Combined with v.15 (stationarity not in non-moving things either), the conclusion is that stationarity, like motion, has no inherent home. It's a dependent designation, not an inherent property.","realLifeExample":"Where is \"silence\"? Not in noise (contradiction). Not in the absence of sound (that's just absence, not inherent silence). Silence is a relative, designated concept, not a thing with its own inherent existence."},{"q":"How does Bohr's complementarity principle work precisely?","a":"Bohr (1928) argued that quantum objects have complementary properties — wave-like (interference, diffraction) and particle-like (definite position, trajectory). A single experiment can reveal one or the other, never both fully simultaneously. The double-slit experiment demonstrates: observe which slit → particle behaviour (no interference). Don't observe → wave behaviour (interference pattern). The measurement context determines which description applies.","realLifeExample":"A person can be a \"friend\" or an \"employee\" to the same person, but in a given interaction, one role dominates. Asking for a favour (friend) and giving a work directive (employer) in the same breath creates confusion — the roles are complementary, not simultaneous."},{"q":"Is this different from superposition?","a":"Yes! Superposition means a system exists in multiple states simultaneously (before measurement). Complementarity means certain descriptions are mutually exclusive (cannot be fully observed together). A qubit CAN be in superposition of states, but you cannot MEASURE both wave and particle aspects simultaneously.","realLifeExample":"A coin spinning in the air is in \"superposition\" (not yet heads or tails). But once it lands, it's either heads OR tails — the outcomes are complementary. Superposition is pre-measurement; complementarity constrains measurement."},{"q":"Does this apply to everyday language?","a":"Yes. Many paired concepts are complementary: hot/cold, moving/stationary, presence/absence. We can't meaningfully assert both simultaneously of the same thing in the same respect. Nāgārjuna uses this to show that these concepts are relational designations, not inherent properties.","realLifeExample":"Is a glass \"half-full\" or \"half-empty\"? You can use either description, but asserting both simultaneously is saying \"it's optimistic AND pessimistic about the same fact in the same way\" — which is contradictory."},{"q":"How does this verse function in the stationarity section?","a":"V.15: stationarity not in moving, non-moving, or third things. The three verses mirror v.1-3's structure applied to rest.","deeper":"The parallel structure (v.1-3 for motion, v.15-17 for rest) shows Nāgārjuna's method is systematic, not ad hoc. Any concept claimed to have inherent existence can be subjected to the same analysis."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Why can't a moving thing be stationary?","options":["A) Because it's too fast","B) Because \"moving\" and \"stationary\" are mutually exclusive — asserting both is a contradiction","C) Because stationary things don't exist","D) Because physics prevents it"],"correct":"B","explanation":"A \"moving thing\" is defined by motion. \"Stationary\" means not-moving. The double-slit experiment shows: observe which slit → particle; don't observe → wave.
